procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 26.03.2010 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in WP No.1212 of 1995.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A Writ Petition (WP No. 1212 of 1995) was filed in the High Court of Delhi challenging SAFEMA proceedings, arguing they became untenable due to the revocation/withdrawal of the detention order passed under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974. In Civil Appeal No. 5500 of 2011, an additional ground was that the criminal complaint had been closed as the appellant was discharged. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on 26.03.2010.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants approached the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed their Writ Petition. They argued that the impugned orders should be quashed because the detention proceedings under COFEPOSA were revoked, the criminal complaint was closed due to the appellant's discharge, and the penalties under the Act of 1962 and the Act of 1968 were also revoked. The Supreme Court is hearing Civil Appeal No. 5500 of 2011 and Criminal Appeal No. 730 of 2014 together, focusing primarily on the facts of the Civil Appeal for brevity.

issue.issue_text: Whether proceedings under the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 would become non est and untenable if the detention order passed under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 is subsequently revoked/withdrawn.

facts: A detention order was passed against the appellant under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 (COFEPOSA).
Consequently, proceedings for forfeiture of property were initiated under the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (SAFEMA).
The detention order was challenged and upheld by the High Court on its merits.
Subsequently, the detention order was revoked by the Union of India based on an undertaking given to the Supreme Court that it would withdraw the order and file a criminal complaint instead.
The appellant argued that because the detention order was revoked, the SAFEMA proceedings were no longer valid or tenable.
law: Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA states that the Act applies to any person against whom a detention order has been made under COFEPOSA.
The proviso to Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA lists specific exceptions, outlining the circumstances under which a revocation or quashing of a detention order would make the SAFEMA proceedings invalid.
application: The Court first established that the initial condition for applying SAFEMA was met, as a detention order *had been made* against the appellant.
The Court then examined the reason for the revocation of the detention order to see if it fell under any of the exceptions listed in the proviso to Section 2(2)(b).
It found that the revocation was not based on the merits of the detention but was the result of a statement made by the Union of India to pursue a criminal complaint instead.

The Court concluded that this specific type of revocation—one made to facilitate a criminal prosecution after the detention order had already been upheld on its merits—is not one of the types of revocation contemplated by the proviso to Section 2(2)(b).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the forfeiture proceedings under SAFEMA do not automatically become untenable upon the revocation of a COFEPOSA detention order. The proceedings only become invalid if the revocation falls within the specific circumstances listed in the proviso to Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA. Since the revocation in this case was not of the type specified in the proviso, the SAFEMA proceedings remained valid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether proceedings under the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 would become non est and untenable if the detention order passed under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974 is subsequently revoked/withdrawn.
appellant_arguments: The proceedings under the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976 (SAFEMA) could not be maintained because the underlying detention order, which is the basis for the SAFEMA proceedings, was subsequently revoked.
respondent_arguments: The revocation of the detention order does not automatically nullify the SAFEMA proceedings. The detention order had been challenged and upheld on its merits by the High Court. The subsequent revocation was made on a statement before the Supreme Court to facilitate the institution of a complaint, which is not a type of revocation that would grant relief to the appellant under Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A revocation of a detention order made on a statement by the government for the procedural purpose of instituting a complaint is not the type of revocation contemplated under Section 2(2)(b) and its proviso, and therefore does not extend a statutory benefit to the detainee, particularly when the detention order has already been upheld on its merits by a competent court.
obiter: The arguments advanced by the learned senior counsel for the appellant appears to be quite attractive and forceful but when the facts and law of the case are scrutinised, we are of the ﬁrm view that argument has to fail.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the revocation of a detention order does not automatically nullify forfeiture proceedings under SAFEMA, especially when the detention order had previously been challenged and upheld on its merits by a High Court. The specific type of revocation in this case, which was made on a statement by the government to facilitate the institution of a separate complaint, is not the kind of revocation contemplated under Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA that would provide relief to the appellant.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of Section 2(2)(b) of the Smugglers and Foreign Exchange Manipulators (Forfeiture of Property) Act, 1976, and its proviso, to determine the types of revocation or setting aside of a detention order that would render SAFEMA proceedings untenable.

Application of the condition in Section 2(2)(b)(iv) of SAFEMA, which requires that a detention order be "set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction" for a person to be excluded from the Act's purview.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's challenge to the detention order had been dismissed on its merits by the High Court, which upheld the order.
The detention order was not "set aside by a court of competent jurisdiction"; it was revoked by the executive branch.

The revocation was made on a statement given by the Union of India before the Supreme Court for the specific purpose of instituting a complaint, not because the detention itself was found to be illegal or improper.
The court found that this specific type of revocation is not one that is contemplated under Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA and its proviso to grant relief from forfeiture proceedings.
why_respondent_won: The detention order had been judicially validated on its merits by the High Court before it was revoked.
The revocation was not a consequence of the detention order being found invalid, but was a procedural step to allow for a different legal action (a complaint).
The conditions under Section 2(2)(b) of SAFEMA for nullifying the proceedings were not met, as the order was never set aside by a competent court.
